outcome: Since 26 January 2024 I found no event bearing on whether there are infinitely many base-2 Carol primes: the largest known Carol index in the sources I could open is still k = 695631 from July 2016, and the only in-window items are analogue searches in other bases seen in search snippets.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many Carol primes, i.e. infinitely many primes of the form (2ⁿ−1)²−2, equivalently 4ⁿ−2ⁿ⁺¹−1 (the 'Carol primes' named by Cletus Emmanuel after Carol G. Kirnon; OEIS A091516). One part only: the statement asks for infinitude. It asks nothing about the indices, sizes, density, distribution or base-b generalisations of these primes. The statement itself does not define 'Carol prime'; the definition is taken from the literature.

events.what_happened: The Prime-Wiki base-2 Carol/Kynea history log, which covers both families together, has the entry 'Found n = 852770, Ryan Propper', dated 2019-07-14. I saw this only in search-result text, because the Prime-Wiki page returned HTTP 503 on every attempt. A Wikipedia-derived Kynea text (mirror, not opened) gives 852770 as the largest known prime Kynea number, 513419 digits, the 51st Kynea prime, found July 2019 with CKSieve and PrimeFormGW.
events.delivers: Not a Carol prime. For n ≡ 2 (mod 3), 2ⁿ ≡ 4 (mod 7), so (2ⁿ−1)²−2 ≡ 3²−2 = 7 ≡ 0 (mod 7), and the value is not prime for n > 2. 852770 ≡ 2 (mod 3), so it is excluded as a Carol index. It is consistent with the Kynea index condition, since Kynea numbers are divisible by 7 only at n ≡ 1 (mod 3). Establishes nothing about Carol primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, unchanged by this entry.
events.directly_checkable: Residue check: 852770 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3, and for n ≡ 2 (mod 3) the value (2ⁿ−1)²−2 is divisible by 7 (for n > 2), so the index cannot give a Carol prime.
events.doubts: The log section that shows this entry covers both families, and the page itself could not be opened. Which family the entry belongs to therefore rests on the mirror text and the residue argument, not on the log line.
events.direction: Not a Carol event; it concerns the Kynea family, which the question does not ask about.

events.revisions: Zenodo lists v9; earlier versions not checked.
events.delivers: Concerns primes n²+1 (Landau's fourth problem), a different problem. It says nothing about (2ⁿ−1)²−2. The name collides because MathWorld's 'near-square prime' page, which defines the Carol primes, uses that phrase for the family of forms n²−k.
events.doubts: Only the abstract was readable, so the argument was not checked. The claim is about a different problem, so no check of it bears on this entry; it is recorded as a discarded neighbour that shares a name.
events.direction: A claimed proof of infinitude for a different family (n²+1). It cuts neither way on Carol primes.

disputes.summary: Largest known Carol-prime index. The Prime Pages curio for index 253987 (Emmanuel, May 2007) still says 'largest known'. OEIS A091515 has later terms up to 695631 (Rodenkirch, 16 July 2016), and the mirrored Wikipedia text gives 695631 as the largest as of April 2020. The curio is superseded by the OEIS record, which I take as the better-supported reading, but I could not confirm that nothing newer has been found.

Index 852770 (Ryan Propper, 14 July 2019) appears in the Prime-Wiki base-2 log, which lists Carol and Kynea entries together. The mirrored Kynea text calls it the largest known Kynea prime. A Carol reading is excluded by the residue argument (852770 ≡ 2 (mod 3), which Carol indices cannot be), so the Kynea attribution rests on that argument and the mirror, not on the log line, which I could not open.

summary: I found nothing in the window that bears on whether there are infinitely many base-2 Carol primes (primes of (2ⁿ−1)²−2). No source I could open says the question is settled: the OEIS entries A091515 and A091516 (opened) list the terms but say nothing about infinitude, MathWorld's Near-Square Prime page (opened) reports 42 known primes as of June 2016 without addressing infinitude, and the HandWiki mirror of the deleted Wikipedia article lists the question as unsolved. The record of new instances in the sources I could open stops at index 695631 (Rodenkirch, 16 July 2016, the 44th OEIS term). The eight OEIS index additions from 2004 to 2016 are recorded as events because the rules require recording old events, though they bear on the family's size, not its infinitude; the term a(39) (a note from 31 March 2006) gives no value. The in-window items are two analogue log entries in other bases (base 10, 20 Feb 2024; base 362, double-check on 29 June 2025), both seen in search snippets only because the Prime-Wiki base-2 page returned HTTP 503 on every attempt. An entry for index 852770 (Ryan Propper, July 2019) sits in the base-2 log that covers both families. I read it as a Kynea prime rather than a Carol prime, because 852770 ≡ 2 (mod 3) and Carol indices in that class give multiples of 7. The English Wikipedia articles 'Carol number' and 'Kynea number' now do not exist. The deletion logs show 'Carol number' was deleted after an articles-for-deletion discussion (second nomination, closed 20 July 2021), recreated repeatedly, and protected on 10 September 2021 ('Repeatedly recreated'); 'Kynea number' was deleted repeatedly in July, August and September 2021 (the July entry cites the Carol articles-for-deletion discussion). The HandWiki and EverybodyWiki 'Carol number' texts (EverybodyWiki returned 403; HandWiki opened in summary) therefore mirror a deleted article, and their 'as of April 2020' record figure is a mirror figure, not a maintained source. The live raw wikitext of 'List of unsolved problems in mathematics', read in full, has 'Are there infinitely many Kynea primes?' under Prime numbers and no Carol bullet. The visible history starts 1 September 2026 and shows no Carol-related edit summary, so I cannot date any removal, and I could not see the frozen January 2024 wording or the bullet's link target. On AI involvement: no source I found names an AI system in connection with Carol primes. The AI-related searches surfaced 2026 prime-adjacent claims, namely an OpenAI preprint on prime gaps at most 186, an Anthropic announcement on the Riemann zeta bound (67.2%), and Erdős-problem items about prime sets. These concern other problems, so I did not record them as events. Close calls: (a) whether the 852770 entry is a Carol record (I say no, on the residue argument); (b) whether the base-10 and base-362 analogues count (under §2.1 they are different questions, so they are recorded as discards); (c) whether the 2004–2016 index additions are events at all (I recorded them, since §5 requires every event to be recorded, but they do not move the infinitude question).
competing_reading: A reader who counts every index addition as progress would say the known family grew from 7 terms in 2004 to 44 terms by July 2016 and that the largest known index moved from 253987 (2007) to 695631 (2016). A reader who counts the base-10 and base-362 entries as in-window activity would say the problem saw work after January 2024. Neither reading moves the infinitude question: new instances do not settle whether the set is infinite, and analogues in other bases are different questions under §2.1. A reader who took the 2019 852770 entry as a Carol record would say the largest known Carol index moved in 2019, but the residue argument rules that out.
what_would_settle_it: The live Prime-Wiki base-2 Carol/Kynea page and its history, which returned 503 throughout this run, to check the 2019 852770 line, any base-2 Carol find after July 2016, and the log's 2020 entries. The Mersenneforum Carol/Kynea search thread and Rodenkirch's search page, for any base-2 Carol find after July 2016. The OEIS A091515 and A091516 revision history after 2024. The frozen 26 January 2024 wikitext of the list, to see the Carol bullet and its link target, and the list's history before 1 September 2026, to date the bullet's removal. A full-text arXiv and Google Scholar search for 'Carol prime' and 'Carol number' in 2024–2026. Steven Harvey's 'Carol and Kynea Primes' file, which OEIS cites.

events.credibility_reason: Claimed proof of Landau's fourth problem known only from an abstract, at v9, with no uptake; in any case a different problem.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many Carol primes exist. Every base-2 index addition (2004–2016) is a finite instance, so each is `instances`. The 852770 entry is a Kynea prime by the residue argument (n ≡ 2 mod 3 gives a multiple of 7), so it is `variant`. Vega's claim is about n²+1 and Sparavigna's paper is about algebraic operations on the numbers, so both are `variant`. The only events after the snapshot are base-10 and base-362 analogue searches, which are `variant`. No event names an AI system.
judgement.doubts: The after-snapshot Prime-Wiki entries and the base-2 log were seen only in search snippets. The research pass could not rule out a base-2 Carol find after July 2016, but even a new one would only be an instance. The live Wikipedia list no longer has the Carol bullet, and the frozen wording and its link target were not seen.
